prompt: Explain population variance to someone who knows averages but no statistics.
oracle: Population variance of [1,3] is 1, mean2, squared units; sample unbiased variance2 for n=2. Squaring is not uniquely forced by avoiding cancellation.
reference: Population variance measures spread that an average alone hides. Assume the complete population is [1,3]; it has mean 2, just like [2,2], but only the first pair is spread out. Its deviations are -1,+1; squared deviations average to (1+1)/2=1 in squared units. Dividing by n-1 instead estimates population variance from a sample; squaring emphasizes large deviations, rather than being the only possible spread measure. Keep the mean and population size fixed and change the distance from the mean: [0,4] gives (4+4)/2=4. Two machines may have the same average delivery time; comparing squared deviations of their complete delivery records reveals which is less consistent.

prompt: Explain opportunity cost for a beginner deciding how to use a free afternoon.
oracle: Value of best forgone alternative, not sum of all alternatives or only money already spent; sunk costs excluded.
reference: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when choosing. Assume you can earn $40 tutoring or enjoy a walk valued at $25 that afternoon; choosing the walk forgoes $40, not $65. A non-refundable fee paid yesterday is a sunk cost. The same time cannot serve both options, so the feasible next-best choice sets the cost, even when the chosen activity costs no cash. Hold the afternoon and walk value fixed; if available tutoring pays only $10, the walk now has a lower opportunity cost. A factory choosing between two products on one machine also sacrifices its best feasible alternative output; an idle machine with no alternative has no such forgone benefit.

prompt: Explain cache invalidation in a web application to a beginner.
oracle: Stale cached copies after origin mutation; TTL vs explicit invalidation; distributed races and eventual freshness, do not claim perfect TTL consistency.
reference: Cache invalidation prevents an old saved result from outliving the change that made it wrong. Imagine a shop caching a product price: an unchanged price is a valid cache hit, but a hit after the database price changes can return stale data. The cache bypasses a database read; deleting or replacing its entry after a price update forces the next read to obtain the new price. A TTL only bounds staleness and does not synchronize all readers. Hold traffic and update timing fixed; shorten the TTL from ten minutes to one minute, reducing the stale window while increasing database reads. A DNS record also has cached copies and expiry: the same origin-change/copy-lifetime relation explains why an address change may take time to appear, though its protocol differs.

prompt: Explain compound growth and why the starting amount matters.
oracle: A=P(1+r)^t fixedrate discreteperiods, P100 r10% t2 =>121, not120; r20%=>144, no guaranteedfinancialreturns.
reference: Compound growth applies each period’s growth to the amount already accumulated. Assume $100 grows at a fixed 10% per year for two years with no withdrawals; simple growth adds $10 each year, while compounding uses the changing balance. A=P(1+r)^t: P is the starting amount, r the per-period rate, and t the number of periods. $100 becomes $110, then $121 because the second gain is $11, not $10. This is a hypothetical calculation, not a promised return. Keep the starting amount and two periods fixed; changing the rate to 20% yields 100×1.2²=$144. A bacterial population under a constant growth factor also multiplies its current size each period; resource limits can break that assumption.

prompt: Explain precision and recall using a small search-result example.
oracle: TP3 FP1 FN2 ->precision3/4 recall3/5; cannot freely assume threshold guaranteesperformance, bothdenominatorsdefinequestion.
reference: Precision asks how many returned results are relevant; recall asks how many relevant results were found. Assume a collection has five relevant documents and a search returns four documents, three relevant. The returned set and the full relevant set are different denominators. Precision is TP/(TP+FP)=3/4; recall is TP/(TP+FN)=3/5. The first measures trust in the returned list, the second coverage of what exists. Keep the collection fixed and add one missed relevant document to the result set without adding irrelevant ones: precision becomes 4/5 and recall 4/5. Removing a relevant result instead loses coverage. A factory’s defect detector can use the same ratios for flagged items and all truly defective items; evaluating recall still requires knowing missed defects.

prompt: Explain idempotency to a developer who is learning distributed systems.
oracle: Repeatedoperation sameeffect not necessarilyresponse; repeatedPUTset vs increment; dedupkeyscope retention atomicity boundaries.
reference: Idempotency means repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once. Setting a record’s state to “closed” twice is idempotent; incrementing its counter twice is not, even if both calls return “OK”. A fixed assignment reaches the same state after repetition, while an increment uses the current state and adds again. For hypothetical retries, a stored request key can suppress duplicate increments if the check and update are atomic. Keep the retried request fixed but expire its stored key: a later retry may increment again, so deduplication only works within its retention and scope. A payment endpoint can store a transaction key to prevent duplicate charges; the same identity/atomic-record relation applies, but identical text alone does not identify the same payment.

prompt: Explain deadlock with a small resource-allocation example.
oracle: Circularwaiting with exclusive locks and holdandwait, consistentordering breakscycle not allcontention; removingone process not alwaysglobalfailure.
reference: Deadlock occurs when waiting tasks prevent one another from making the progress needed to release resources. Assume task A holds exclusive lock X and waits for Y, while B holds Y and waits for X. One task waiting for a lock that another will soon release is ordinary contention, not this cycle. Neither can continue to its release step: A needs B’s resource and B needs A’s. The exclusive locks and hold-while-waiting rule sustain the cycle. Keep the two tasks and resources, but require both to acquire X before Y: B cannot hold Y while waiting for X, breaking this cycle while contention remains. Two trains occupying sections and each waiting for the other’s section can share the same exclusive-resource waiting cycle; actual railway rules determine whether that model applies.

reference: 公共物品的关键是使用通常不减少别人可用的份额，也难把未付费者排除。 在简化情境中，一盏街灯照亮整条街，多一个行人不明显减少照明，收费排除路人也难；免费发的一份面包会被吃掉，不能因此算公共物品。 每人都能受益却难单独收费，有人便可能等待别人出钱，导致私人筹资不足；这并不证明无人会自愿贡献。 保持照明服务不变，只让街区可通过门禁排除未付费者，就改变了排他性，成为更接近俱乐部物品的安排。 公开的防灾警报也可能满足共同使用和难排除两项条件；若系统只向付费设备发送，排他条件便不同。

prompt: Explain Little’s law for an introductory queueing class.
oracle: L=lambda W stable longrun matchingboundaries units;2customers/min*3min=6; noPoissonneeded, waitingtimeversussystemtime match.
reference: Little’s law connects the average number in a stable system to the arrival rate and average time spent there. Assume a stable café averages two customer arrivals per minute and three minutes from entry to exit. Customers in the café and customers only waiting in line are different system boundaries. L=λW gives 2 customers/minute × 3 minutes = 6 customers on average. Each arrival contributes its residence time, so the long-run accumulated customer-time divided by observation time yields the same average occupancy; no Poisson assumption is required. Hold arrival rate and the stable café boundary fixed; reduce average residence to two minutes and L becomes four customers. Stable network requests in flight obey the same rate-times-latency relation, provided latency and request count refer to the same boundary and arrivals do not exceed sustainable service.
